analysis.one_liner: Strengthens penalties, enforcement, and pay-data collection to fight sex-based wage discrimination.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 208 House cosponsors, 207 of them Democrats, but never received a House vote and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Equal Pay Act so employers can only justify paying a woman less than a man for similar work using real, job-related reasons like education, training, or experience — not 'any factor other than sex.' It would let workers recover compensatory and, in some cases, punitive damages, join class-action lawsuits without signing on individually, and protect workers who ask about or share wage information from being fired. It would also require federal agencies to collect employer pay data by sex, race, and national origin, and run training and outreach programs.
analysis.who_benefits: Women who are paid less than male colleagues for comparable work would gain stronger legal tools: easier lawsuits, bigger possible awards, class actions, and protection against retaliation for discussing pay. Their families benefit from higher household earnings, and the bill funds salary-negotiation training for girls and women.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Women facing pay discrimination and their families

how_it_helps.text: Limits the defenses employers can use for paying women less to 'bona fide' factors like education, training, or experience, and requires the employer to prove the factor is job-related and consistent with business necessity [S2][S3].

Adds liability for compensatory damages, and punitive damages where the employer acted with malice or reckless indifference, and allows equal pay cases to proceed as class actions with expert fees recoverable [S2][S3].
Prohibits employers from retaliating against workers who inquire about, discuss, or disclose wages — in response to a complaint, in a proceeding, or in an employer's own investigation [S2][S3].

Directs the EEOC to issue regulations collecting pay information from employers broken down by sex, race, and national origin, for use in enforcing pay discrimination laws, and funds negotiation-skills training and small-business compliance help [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers — primarily businesses large enough to be covered by the Fair Labor Standards Act — would bear the cost: higher exposure to damages awards and class-action litigation, new pay-data reporting requirements, and potentially higher wages where pay gaps cannot be justified.

drawbacks.text: Employers would face greater litigation exposure, including punitive damages and class actions, which raises legal costs and settlement pressure even for employers who believe their pay practices are legitimate [S2][S3].
The bill itself directs the EEOC to weigh 'the imposition of burdens on employers' in designing its new pay-data collection, acknowledging that mandated reporting adds real compliance work [S3].

Replacing the broad 'any factor other than sex' defense with a stricter 'business necessity' standard narrows employers' ability to defend pay differences based on market rates, prior salaries, or individualized arrangements — a change critics viewed as making legitimate distinctions harder to defend [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, the benefit is a realistic path to challenge pay discrimination that today is often hard to prove, with real money damages attached. The costs — more lawsuits and data reporting — fall on employers, and honest supporters should acknowledge that the punitive-damages and class-action provisions raise litigation costs for businesses of all sizes, including ones acting in good faith. The bill tries to soften that with small-business exemptions tied to the Fair Labor Standards Act and free compliance materials, but the compliance burden is genuine. On balance, the bill's core is a worker-side remedy, and its cost is a business-side one.

outcome.mechanism: The House Labor Committee never acted on the bill, a discharge petition to force it out of committee fell short of the 218 signatures needed, and the bill died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 23, 2013 and referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce [S1][S5].
It gathered 208 cosponsors — 207 Democrats and 1 Republican [S4].

On April 11, 2013, Rep. DeLauro filed a discharge petition (Petition No. 113-1) to force the bill out of committee and onto the floor; a discharge petition needs a majority of the House, 218 signatures, to work [S5].
Twelve days later, on April 23, 2013, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, and no further action was taken [S5].
The bill never received a floor vote in either chamber and died when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers are better off because the bill died: they avoided expanded damages liability, class-action exposure, and new pay-data reporting. Workers facing pay discrimination gained nothing, since the bill never became law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers who avoided new liability and reporting

for.name: Rep. Rosa DeLauro
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and filed Discharge Petition No. 113-1 to force it out of committee for a floor vote

for.name: President Barack Obama
for.what_they_did: Publicly pressed Congress to pass the Paycheck Fairness Act, including in his 2014 State of the Union address

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce (Chair John Kline)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill; instead referred it to a subcommittee on April 23, 2013, where it stayed

against.name: House Republicans who declined to sign the discharge petition
against.role: Needed 218 signatures to force a floor vote; the petition fell short
against.what_they_did: Did not provide the signatures required to bring the bill to the floor over the committee's inaction

against.name: U.S. Chamber of Commerce
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill, arguing it would expand litigation and burdens on employers

sides.party_line_note: 207 of the bill's 208 cosponsors were Democrats and 1 was a Republican; with Republicans holding the House majority and the committee chairship, the bill never reached the floor.

industries.industry: Covered employers (businesses subject to the Fair Labor Standards Act)
industries.note: The bill would have exposed employers to compensatory and punitive damages, class-action equal pay suits, and a new pay-data reporting requirement. Its interest in avoiding that liability ran against workers' interest in enforceable equal pay.

The bill exempts small businesses to the same extent they are exempt from the Fair Labor Standards Act and directs federal agencies to produce free compliance materials, but it still funds training programs and would raise labor standards in the markets small employers compete in.

industries.industry: Labor unions and women's advocacy organizations
industries.note: Stronger equal pay enforcement and wage-transparency protections align with these groups' organizing goals, and the bill provides information and grant programs they could participate in.
